thread.title: My advice on lowering your truck static.
thread.first_post_html:
Long post ahead. I got a PM and see many threads addressing questions about how to go about static drops and how they work in real life, so I thought I would make a post putting my .02 cents in, having driven a 96 chevy extended cab slammed 5/8 every day for 8 months now, day in and day out.

I'm going to give you all some good advice, because I have learned a lot working on my truck, doing all the work myself, and having to rely on it for sole transportation (which can be tricky at times like now, when its down most of the time for a full custom paint job ) . Anyway, as far as the suspension goes, I was/am in the same boat as you. I started with a 3/4 drop, and while it was cool and very streetable, I didn't like the rake too much. I wanted bags, couldn't afford it at the time. The reason I went with the 5/8 was because I already had the 3" coils and 2" hangers. That was mistake #1. Hangers. They are a total pain. You have to pull the bed to put them on and the rivets on the driver's side are blocked by the gas tank. So, I went my merry way to the local hot rod shop and picked up a 6" flip kit and 2" lower control arms. Mistake #2. LCAs + coils = alignment issues. I'm going to swap them out for spindles, and I will be able to align it all back to spec, and they wont rub the inner lip of my $600 apiece wheels like they do now Now, a 4/6 is a very streetable drop. The only real thing you have to cut is the frame for the bolt in notch. Sure, a 4/6 is cool.. but you want to go that extra mile right? I did. So, when you take the plunge and go 5/8 ( you know you want to) you'll want to use 3" coils and 2" spindles in the front, and a flipkit and shackles in the back. You could think that you'll be okay on the bolt in notch like I did, but you'll hate it instantly. There's no travel. So, knowing that I will want bags later, i went ahead and cut the bed out and welded in a monster notch from Suicidedoors.com . But, if you dont want the big hole and dont care about laying out all the way, get the same notch i did ( the 8" one ) and just trim it down to fit under the bed floor. I have plenty of travel in my notch, I can lay frame on 22s easy. Now, for the front, anything lower than 4" and you have to cut a notch in the frame for your tie rod ends. If those break youre screwed. You'll also notice your swaybar doesnt fit. Dont chunk it - I ran without it for a while and yes, it does make a big difference in these big trucks. What you'll need is some shorter endlinks. However, if you use DJM lca's, you'll notice that their brilliant engineering department designed them so that the swaybar is at some goofy angle and you end up busting out your bushings. Solution = redrill and tap the swaybar mounts on the frame. Also, dont forget your carrier bearing shim. Nothing is worse than taking off from a stop and getting that extra vibration jiggling your hot, expensive Starbucks all over your dash. If you go 5" in the front, and even with a wheel and tire combo that equals 27" in overall diameter like my 20s with 255/35ZR20 tires, you'll need to cut out or better yet modify your inner fenders in the front, cause rubbing them and bumping them sucks. And for peace of mind, even though my billet Intro wheels tuck perfectly, I rolled all 4 of my fender lips - no worries. And if your roads even slightly suck like they do here, you'll want a slightly larger profile tire, like a 45 or 50 series, something in there. Good luck, and remember - No fat chicks, the truck will scrape!

Cody

Originally posted by thecodeman
anything lower than 4" and you have to cut a notch in the frame for your tie rod ends.

I disagree, I'm way lower then 4" in the front and mine don't hit. Nor do Matty's and I just did a 5" drop on his on Sat.

The only problem I have with the 5-7 is the ss has a 14bolt rear so the pumkin hits the bed on large bumps, it might even be cause the 3" exhaust pipes run over the rear, but no problems in the front at all. I drove it 58 miles from Doogies and then cruised around my crappy streets for a few hours yesterday and still no problem with the front.
Are your tierods hitting or are the sleaves hitting. If the sleaves are hitting, you can rotate the, so the bolts don't hit.

Originally posted by CKTA
Are your tierods hitting or are the sleaves hitting. If the sleaves are hitting, you can rotate the, so the bolts don't hit.
I will post pics in a second.

Here is a before pic:


And here is an after pic:
Ouch! All you had to do was rotate the adjustment sleave!:LOL:

Originally posted by CKTA
Ouch! All you had to do was rotate the adjustment sleave!:LOL:
No, I did that at first, and that whole outer sleeve was scraping. Had I left it alone, they would have gotten bent against the frame and then you're fubared without steering

Originally posted by CKTA
Ouch! All you had to do was rotate the adjustment sleave!:LOL:
BTW, where the hell is the sway bar?

Originally posted by thecodeman
No, I did that at first, and that whole outer sleeve was scraping. Had I left it alone, they would have gotten bent against the frame and then you're fubared without steering
Maybe the stock spindles are making it do that.

Originally posted by CKTA
BTW, where the hell is the sway bar?
That was during the part of my first post where I mentioned it doesn't fit worth a crap and I drove without it:clown:

Originally posted by CKTA
Maybe the stock spindles are making it do that.
Could be, thats why I want to redo the front with spindles.
Has to be the stock spindles.

I'm with dougie on this one. mine was 6-8 for well over 3 years. I never had a problem with my sway bar or my tie rods.

The only major problem I had was my y pipe got a little dinged, and my gas tank sheild was a little scraped....other than that..not a single problem in 3 years

Yeah, it's definately the spindles....even on my '94 the tierods are almost level.....look at Codemans, his are on a pretty good angle because the stock spindle mounting hieght. That 2" spindle makes all the differance in the world I guess.
How the hell did you two 's manage to cause a tranny problem while working on the suspension...

Originally posted by justin
How the hell did you two 's manage to cause a tranny problem while working on the suspension...

I guess his yoke shaft (insert g@y joke here) was rusty and when the driveshaft went into the seal further it caused it to seap out some. No problems.......I was just figuing the worst..... as usual. I already had it in my mind i was going home to get the '96 and tow him back to my house.

The 2" lca's push the tierod mount up(on the spindles). A 2" dropped spindle keeps the stock tie rod mount. I was rollin a 6.5" drop up front, with no scraping of the tie rods at all. Now I'm rollin a 5.5" front drop daily with no scraping.

Fender wells-pull them out. I hit them all day long.
DJM cnotch-not worth a crap over a 6" drop
shock extenders- a must have
bed support over the differential-trim it so the diff doesnt hit
DJM coils- not meant for extended cab v8's. Stick with belltech's
Adjustable shackles- man's best friend
Hangers- man's worst enemy
y pipe- Get it raised if you go over a 4" drop.
exhaust in rear- dump it before the axle if using a 7" drop and up

This is a little of my advise in slamming your truck. A 4/7 drop is prolly the lowest you wanna go without cutting crap up. My bag stuff is ordered, so this low static crap is outta here.

Originally posted by Beyond Static©

DJM coils- not meant for extended cab v8's. Stick with belltech's
Funny, my DJM's have been in for 6 years now. No problems.
My coils must have been duds. They slammed me 4.5" up front. StylinConcepts said nothing about a special coil for the v8 or extended cab. The coils made me come exactly 1" from tucking rim up front.

Originally posted by 5-8CHEVY
I've flipped them and the tie rod sleeves still hit the frame. I think it has more to do with the arms than anything since Cody is having the same issues but you guys with spindles aren't.
I'm thinking the same thing since I haven't heard a problem with a 5" drop with spindles and springs.


BTW
There is no tranny leak I just checked to make sure, it had to be cause you had it jacked up in the front all that time.

Originally posted by Beyond Static©
My coils must have been duds. They slammed me 4.5" up front. StylinConcepts said nothing about a special coil for the v8 or extended cab. The coils made me come exactly 1" from tucking rim up front.
That's why I like Belltech coils, they are made just for the 454ss and ext cab to hold the weight, I used hotckis 2" coils on my wifes ss and it dropped it about 3.5"

joe

rewrite.rewritten_title: Tips for Lowering Your Truck’s Static Height
rewrite.summary: This thread provides insights from a truck owner who went through various modifications to lower his 96 Chevy extended cab by 5/8 of an inch. The discussion covers necessary components, potential issues, and recommendations.
rewrite.rewritten_article_markdown:
This post shares valuable insights from a truck owner who lowered his 96 Chevy extended cab by 5/8 of an inch. Starting with a 3/4 drop, he eventually opted for a more aggressive 5/8 drop to improve the stance and ride quality. Here are some key points to consider:

- **Starting Equipment**: The author initially used 3-inch coils and 2-inch hangers but found them problematic. He recommends using 3" coils and 2" spindles in the front, with a flip kit and shackles in the back.

- **Front Suspension Issues**: For lower drops than 4 inches (such as a 5/8 drop), cutting a notch in the frame for tie rod ends is necessary to avoid scraping. The author mentions that his truck has plenty of travel in the frame notch, allowing him to lay down on 22-inch wheels easily.

- **Sway Bar Considerations**: Using the stock sway bar can lead to issues with fit and function. The author suggests removing it temporarily but acknowledges its importance for stability. He recommends redesigning the swaybar mounts or using shorter endlinks if DJM spindles are used.

- **Notch Modifications**: The author opted for a 8-inch notch from Suicidedoors.com, which he claims provides plenty of travel for his truck.

- **Customization and Adjustments**: Proper alignment is crucial after installing new components. The author mentions issues with the swaybar fit due to the DJM spindles but found that redrilling the mounts resolved the problem.

- **Wheels and Tires**: For optimal performance, he suggests using 45 or 50 series tires on roads with poor conditions.

post_rewrites.rewritten_content:
I recently drove a 1996 Chevy Extended Cab Slam 5/8 for 8 months daily and can share valuable insights on static drops. While a 3/4 drop is streetable, I found the rake unsatisfactory and opted for a 5/8 drop due to existing 3" coils and 2" hangers, which turned out to be a mistake. The hangers required a bed pull, and driver-side rivets were blocked by the gas tank.

Mistake #2: I installed 6" flip kits with lower control arms (LCAs). This led to alignment issues. Now, swapping for spindles will correct this, preventing wheel rub.

A 4/6 drop is streetable but lacking in travel. For a full 5/8 drop, use 3" coils and 2" spindles in the front with a flip kit and shackles in the rear. Cutting a frame notch for tie rod ends or swaybar compatibility is necessary; redrill swaybar mounts if using DJM LCAs to avoid bushing damage.

Ensure a carrier bearing shim to eliminate vibration, especially when starting. For 27" overall diameter tires like mine, modify inner fenders in the front to prevent rubbing and ensure fender lips are rolled for peace of mind.

In areas with poor roads, opt for slightly larger profile tires (45-50 series) for comfort. Remember, no fat chicks—this truck will scrape!

Thecodeman originally stated that anything below 4 inches would require cutting a notch in the frame for tie rod ends. However, I disagree; both my vehicle and Matty’s are significantly lower than 4 inches, and we haven't encountered any issues. In fact, we just completed a 5-inch drop on Matty's vehicle last Saturday.

The only issue with the 5-7 is that its 14-bolt rear causes the pumpkin to hit the bed on large bumps, though there are no problems in the front. After driving it 58 miles and cruising through my streets, I haven't encountered any issues with the front end.
Are the tierods hitting or the sleeves? If the sleeves are causing interference, you can adjust their position to ensure the bolts do not collide.
Are the tierods or sleeve boots causing interference? If it's the sleeve boots, you can adjust them to prevent bolt contact. I'll post some pictures shortly.
Before and after photos are provided below.
All you needed to do was rotate the adjustment sleeve.laughs

Originally posted by CKTA: Ouch! All you had to do was rotate the adjustment sleeve. Initially, I tried adjusting the outer sleeve, which was scraping. If I hadn't corrected it, the components would have rubbed against the frame, potentially damaging the steering system.

Originally posted by CKTA: Ouch! All you had to do was rotate the adjustment sleeve.

Originally posted by thecodeman: I encountered similar issues. Initially, rotating the outer sleeve caused scraping. If I hadn't adjusted it, the sleeves would have bent against the frame, leaving me without steering. Maybe the stock spindles are contributing to this problem.

Originally posted by CKTA

In my first post, I mentioned that the sway bar doesn't fit properly and had to drive without it. Originally posted by CKTA

Maybe the stock spindles are causing this issue. That’s why I plan to replace them as part of the front suspension redo.
The issue is likely with the stock spindles.

I agree with dougie. My vehicle's sway bar and tie rods have been stable for over three years, showing no issues. The only minor problems were a slightly dented y-pipe and a scuffed gas tank shield. Otherwise, the car has been flawless for three years.

The issue is definitely with the spindles. Even on my '94 model, the tie rods are nearly parallel. Codeman's setup has a slight angle due to the stock spindle height. It seems the 2-inch spindles make a significant difference.
How did you manage to introduce a transmission issue while working on the suspension?

Originally posted by Justin: How did you manage to cause a transmission issue while working on the suspension? I guess the yoke shaft was rusty, and when the driveshaft went deeper into the seal, it caused leakage. No big deal... I was worried the worst, as usual. I was already planning to tow his '96 back to my house.

For a 2-inch lift, the lower control arm (LCA) pushes the tie rod mount upward on the spindles. A 2-inch drop spindle maintains the stock tie rod mount. With a 6.5-inch front drop, there was no tie rod scraping. Now, using a 5.5-inch daily drop also prevents scraping.

Fender wells need to be moved outward to avoid contact. I encountered them frequently throughout the day.

For a 6-inch drop shock absorber extenders are essential; differential support is crucial for extended cab V8s. Use Belltech Adjustable Shackles for better alignment and clearance. Hangers can cause issues with clearance.

A Y-pipe should be raised if you have more than a 4-inch drop. In the rear, dump the exhaust before the axle for drops of 7 inches or greater.

A 4- to 7-inch drop is generally advisable without cutting into components. My ordered low/static components will be removed.

Originally posted by Beyond Static: The coils are not designed for extended cab V8s. For reliable performance, consider Belltech's options. My DJM units, which have been installed for six years, have had no issues.

The coil springs I used caused excessive lift, raising the front end by 4.5 inches. According to StylinConcepts, no specific coil was required for the V8 or extended cab model. These springs resulted in a 1-inch intrusion close to the tire rim at the front.

Originally posted by 5-8CHEVY: The tie rod sleeves still hit the frame after flipping them, suggesting an issue with the arms rather than the spindles or springs, as Cody is experiencing similar problems but others with spindles have not reported issues. Originally posted by Beyond Static©: My coils were likely defective, causing a 4.5" drop up front. StylinConcepts did not specify special coils for V8 or extended cab models. The coils pushed me to within 1" of rim tucking. Belltech coils, designed for the 454SS and extended cab, performed better, while Hotchkis 2" coils dropped my wife’s SS about 3.5".

I have a question about a 4/6 drop for my '96 Silverado extended cab. I found one priced at $399 that includes spindles, springs, and a rear flip kit. Is this a good price? How will the ride be with this setup? Also, do you have a picture of your truck with the 5/8 drop? Thanks for the help!

-Joe
